## Problem 1

```{r}
# Set birthday function
birthday_sim = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Simulate birthdays and check whether at least two people share a birthday
birthday_sim(10)
birthday_sim(23)
birthday_sim(50)
```

```{r}
set.seed(123)

# Estimate the probability for each group size using 10,000 simulations
birthday_results = 
  tibble(group_size = 2:50) |>
  mutate(
    probability = map_dbl(
      group_size,
      \(n) mean(replicate(10000, birthday_sim(n)))
    )
  )

birthday_results
```

```{r birthday_plot}
# Plot the estimated probability of a shared birthday by group size
birthday_results |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 1.5) +

  # Add a reference line at 50% probability
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.5,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +

  # Customize labels and axis scales
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a Shared Birthday by Group Size",
    x = "Group Size",
    y = "Probability of Shared Birthday"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 50, 5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The simulation results show that the probability of at least two people sharing a birthday increases as group size increases. With 10 people, the estimated probability is `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 10) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)`, while with 23 people, it reaches `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 23) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)`, exceeding 50% despite the relatively small group size. As the group size increases further, the probability rises to `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 30) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)` for 30 people and `r scales::percent(birthday_results |> filter(group_size == 50) |> pull(probability), accuracy = 0.01)` for 50 people. These findings illustrate the birthday paradox, demonstrating that shared birthdays become likely even in moderately sized groups.



## Problem 2

```{r}
# List all CSV files in the data directory
file_names = list.files(
  path = "data",
  pattern = "\\.csv$",
  full.names = TRUE
)

# Check the number of files and inspect their names
length(file_names)
head(file_names)
```

```{r}
# Inspect the structure of an individual participant's data
example_subject = read_csv(file_names[1], show_col_types = FALSE)

glimpse(example_subject)
head(example_subject)
```

```{r}
# Create a dataframe of file names and read each participant's data
longitudinal_files =
  tibble(file_name = file_names) |>
  mutate(
    subject_data = map(
      file_name,
      \(file) read_csv(file, show_col_types = FALSE)
    )
  )

# Inspect the resulting dataframe and list-column
glimpse(longitudinal_files)
```

```{r}
# Extract subject IDs and treatment arms from file names
longitudinal_data =
  longitudinal_files |>
  mutate(
    file_id = basename(file_name),
    arm = case_when(
      str_starts(file_id, "con") ~ "Control",
      str_starts(file_id, "exp") ~ "Experimental"
    ),
    subject_id = str_extract(file_id, "\\d+")
  ) |>

  # Expand the participant data stored in the list-column
  unnest(subject_data) |>

  # Convert weekly observations from wide to long format
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.integer(str_remove(week, "week_")),
    arm = factor(arm, levels = c("Control", "Experimental"))
  ) |>

  # Keep only the variables needed for analysis
  select(subject_id, arm, week, observation) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

# Check the dimensions and structure of the tidy dataset
dim(longitudinal_data)
glimpse(longitudinal_data)
head(longitudinal_data)
```

```{r spaghetti_plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
# Plot individual trajectories over time for each treatment arm
longitudinal_data |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = observation,
      group = subject_id
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(color = subject_id),
    linewidth = 0.7,
    alpha = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = subject_id),
    size = 1.5
  ) +

  # Display control and experimental groups separately
  facet_wrap(~ arm) +

  # Customize labels and plot appearance
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  labs(
    title = "Individual Trajectories Over Time by Treatment Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Subject ID"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```

The spaghetti plot shows distinct longitudinal patterns between the control and experimental groups. In the control group, observations fluctuate over the eight weeks without a clear overall increasing or decreasing trend. In contrast, most subjects in the experimental group exhibit an upward trajectory, with observations generally increasing over time. By the later weeks, observations in the experimental group tend to be higher than those in the control group. Although individual variability is present in both groups, the experimental group demonstrates a more pronounced positive trend, suggesting a possible effect of the experimental intervention.
